title: Covid-Era Babies Are "Talking" Less, Signaling Future Reading Challenges
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler reports on two studies, one from LENA and one from Brown University's baby imaging lab, suggesting that babies born during the pandemic vocalize less and experience fewer adult-child conversational turns. Because conversational turns are a key predictor of school readiness and language drives vocabulary and reading, she argues that the Covid learning-loss problem extends down to infants and toddlers. The drop was steepest in the bottom quarter of families by socioeconomic status, whose children will likely need help from schools as well as parents. Rather than adding tutoring burdens, she argues that schools should change curriculum and instruction, moving from haphazard to systematic phonics and building academic knowledge and vocabulary from kindergarten through read-alouds and discussion. She criticises comprehension skills-and-strategies instruction on random topics, citing the cognitive-science finding that substantive knowledge matters more than skills. She concludes that pandemic strain should not be an excuse to keep an approach to reading instruction that has been failing students.
points: LENA and Brown studies found fewer vocalizations and conversational turns among pandemic-born babies, with the steepest declines in the bottom socioeconomic quartile.
Conversational turns are a key predictor of school readiness, so early language deficits become reading challenges later.
The most practical school response is to adopt systematic phonics and foundational skills instruction rather than rely on tutoring alone.
Literacy curricula need to build knowledge and academic vocabulary from kindergarten, because written language uses syntax and words rarely found in conversation.
Skills-and-strategies comprehension practice cannot compensate for missing background knowledge and vocabulary.
quotes: Because of Covid-related disruptions, about a third of early elementary students will likely need intensive support to become proficient readers, according to one study. Now two additional studies suggest that many children born during the pandemic will also be at risk for academic failure. It seems that overburdened parents haven’t been able to engage babies and toddlers in the kind of “conversation” that is crucial for language development—and eventually, for reading.

In addition, the device can calculate the number of “conversational turns”—brief episodes of back-and-forth dialogue—in which the child engages. Research has shown that the number of conversational turns affects brain development and is a key predictor of children’s school readiness, social-emotional development, and other life outcomes.

One year into the pandemic, researchers found that children’s average cognitive performance was the lowest it had been since the study began. A separate analysis of infants found a dramatic decline in verbal functioning in 2021, apparently because adults were initiating fewer conversational turns.

While the decline in verbal interaction has affected all socioeconomic groups, both studies show that the drop has been most dramatic among the bottom 25%. In the LENA study, children in that group went from the 45th percentile to the 25th in the number of their conversational turns. To compensate for the effects of the pandemic, those children will likely need help not just from their families but also from their schools.

One basic change that is gathering steam across the country is to switch from a haphazard approach to instruction in phonics and other foundational reading skills to one that is systematic. Not all children need systematic phonics in order to learn to decipher words fluently, but many and perhaps most do—especially those at the lower end of the socioeconomic spectrum.

Conversational turns are important in early language development, but written language uses sophisticated vocabulary and syntax that are rarely found in conversation. To prepare young children to understand the kind of text they’ll encounter in later years, their “conversational turns” need to start including more elevated language.

But, as cognitive scientists have long known, when it comes to comprehension, substantive knowledge is far more important than “skills.” If students lack knowledge of the topic or of academic vocabulary in general, no amount of practice in “finding the main idea” will enable them to understand complex text.
